Boundaries of Form and Subject in Fifteenth-Century dits

Helen Swift

University of Oxford

There is significant continuity in the late-medieval dit, the most popular form of first-

person narrative courtly poetry in French. There are also, however, certain 15th century

developments that raise in new ways important questions about boundaries of selfhood and self-

definition in the dit: what constitutes the borders of a first-person subject? What are the

parameters of “narrative” as an operable category in relation to “lyric” and “discursive”? These

developments lie in “arguably the most significant courtly poetic phenomenon in the fifteenth

century” (Hult 779): Alain Chartier’s Belle Dame sans Mercy (1424, BDSM), the poetic debate

that it generated over the next half-century, and the legacy of Chartier’s influence attested by

continued reception of the querelle into early print (Bouchet, “A Good Carter as Guide”).

BDSM generates three first-person subjects through its scenario of overheard debate: the

lover, the lady, and the narrator. All three are elaborated in literary responses to the poem, with

slippages between lover and narrator being developed in ways that promote malleable

boundaries of subject-hood so as to offer fresh perspectives on the courtly love situation (Swift

91-120). I consider three responses – Achille Caulier’s La Cruelle femme en amour (1430), and

two anonymous dits: Le Debat sans conclusion (before 1460), and Le Purgatoire d’amours

(1463) – which feature together in the first anthology of dits and lyrics to appear in print in

France, Le Jardin de plaisance et fleur de rethorique (1501, JdP). Anthologisation introduces

further boundary negotiation: framing intertextuality as material interaction through co-textual

juxtaposition and rubrication; embedding individual dits in overarching adumbrated narrative

and discursive frameworks; and, in the case of JdP, collating as a single item several rondeaux

by Chartier, framing lyric as narrative.


<!-- Page 2 -->


2

This chapter’s group of related texts thus interrogates in a quite particular way the

situationality of first-person narration and the limitations of perspective in the first person. The

allegorical dimension of its dits is variable, both in the extent to which it is deployed for

discursive or narrative elaboration, and the ways in which it serves, in conjunction with

mythological material, to question the relationship between particular and universal human

experience. Finally, that JdP was produced for an audience of Parisian jurist amateur poets also

usefully challenges any false dichotomy between courtly and urban in the reception of late-

medieval dits (Taylor 258-60).

Relational identity in BDSM

BDSM stages a voluble, self-styled amant martir suitor (l’Amant) being rejected by an

allegedly merciless, rhetorically adroit lady (la Dame) in a debate of some seventy-two

octosyllabic huitains, overheard through a trellis by a narrator (l’Acteur) whose twenty-eight

stanzas book-end the poem with self-presentation, observation, and commentary. It is important

not to diminish retrospectively the complexity of Chartier’s original poem: scholarship on the

querelle frequently notes that the responses “develop increasingly elaborate narrative settings”

(Armstrong and Kay 143); whilst it is true that the narrative content of BDSM is quite simple,

its narratorial self-presentation and discursive positioning are as sophisticated as any of the later

contributions. L’Acteur introduces himself in terms of superlative singularity as a bereaved

lover, “le plus doulent des amoureux” (4: “the saddest of lovers”);1 having asserted a declining

amorous identity, he then depicts an unraveling writerly identity (“[…] il fault que je cesse / De

ditter…”, [9-10: “[…] I must stop / the writing”]) accompanied by embodied dislocation and

impotence affecting “langue,” “bouche,” “yeulx,” “cuer” (20-23: “tongue, mouth, eyes, heart”).

In testamentary vein, presenting himself as left-over and discomposed (“[La Mort] me laisse

seul,” [7: “[Death] left me alone”]), he leaves to others the possibility of composition (“Je laisse

[…] / Faire chançons, dis, et balades,” [25, 27: “I leave […] / to write and sing songs and


<!-- Page 3 -->


3

ballades”]; “Je laisse aux aultres amans faire,” [35: “I leave it to others to take over”]). BDSM’s

narratorial first person thus effortfully distinguishes himself from others, whilst simultaneously

situating himself in relation to them; and the “himself” that he delineates is not itself a pre-

formed, coherent identity, but a subjecthood in formation (or, indeed, deformation).

BDSM’s Acteur can be seen to carry the legacy of myriad disconsolate first-persons of

earlier generations of dit poets, but it also inherits its identity more specifically from Chartier’s

Complainte de la mort a la dame M. Alain,2 with “La Mort m’a tollu ma maistresse” (6: “Death

has taken my mistress from me”) echoing in the third person the second-person invective

opening the Complainte’s second stanza: “Tu m’a osté ma dame et ma mistresse” (13: “You

took from me my lady and my mistress”). Such intertextual relationality adumbrates a certain

autobiographicality, intersecting narratorial and authorial identities – a productively refractive

ambiguity, seen much in Machaut, on which Chartier capitalizes when he playfully assumes

conflation of the extratextual and intratextual levels in L’Excusacion de Maistre Alain, the

ironic non-apology for BDSM that its first-person claims he was compelled to write to redress

court upset in response to the earlier poem. A further aspect of relationality emerges when

BDSM’s Acteur encounters the courtly gathering at which he will overhear the debate. Unable

to adopt the distanced-observer posture that he would prefer (“me retrehÿ voulentiers,” [57: “I

withdrew myself willingly”]), he is instead obliged by friends to participate, and thus to perform

an identity that ill suits his self-marginalizing self-stylization. But he espies someone else whom

he construes to be doing likewise: “ung entre les aultres” (81: “one [among the others]”)

similarly disconsolately distracted, who nonetheless “son semblant fort contretenoit” (85: “he

tried to control the expression of his face”) and “menoit une joie fainte” (90: “ke[pt] his

countenance gay”); first-person identity is both self-perception and self-projection. The espied

individual is anonymous, “le noir portoit en sa devise” (102: “he was dressed all in black, with

no crest to identify him”), and l’Acteur makes explicit their interrelation: “autel fus je comme

vous estez” (120: “I was once as you are now”). His pronouncement uses a formulation from


<!-- Page 4 -->


4

dialogues of Les Trois Morts et les Trois Vifs, when the Dead confront the Living with their

mortal destiny; it thereby suits thematically, albeit with a tinge of macabre irony, l’Amant’s

amant martir rhetoric and l’Acteur’s tone of testamentary valediction. Maintaining the

formula’s first-person collective form (“nous”) presents l’Acteur’s and l’Amant’s “je”s as

intersecting and mutually constitutive entities, circulating neither as universal generality nor as

particularised individuality. An essential foundation of querelle subjecthood is established: the

relationality of first-person identity, which is thereafter demonstrated through l’Acteur’s

account of the love debate from his eavesdropping position, sight obscured but audition barely

impeded: “Et n’y avoit aultre destour / Fors la treille entre moy et eulx” (167-8: “And there was

no other barrier but the trellis to separate them from me”).

After reporting the discussion, l’Acteur intervenes as judge of the interlocutors

themselves, asserting a discursive authority that he seemingly abrogated before, thereby

implying that the act of recounting (the “dire” that he claimed to abandon) has itself

reconstituted his subjecthood. The activity of judgment was earlier portended in a curious and

otherwise undeveloped observation by l’Acteur at the gathering that:

telz y ot qui a ce jour virent

En la compaignie leans

leurs juges […]

Qui les tiennent en leurs liens (77-80)

[“some saw there that day / among the company assembled, / their judges […], / who

held them in thrall”].

The indefinite “telz” thus appears retrospectively to imply l’Amant and la Dame, just as

the second “qui” emerges as l’Acteur. In the poem’s final two stanzas, he imposes two verdicts,

both indirect and formulated as invocations: one to lovers and one to ladies. Lovers are exhorted

to eschew “ces vanteurs et ces mesdisans” (786: “these braggarts and scandalmongers”); the

referent corresponding to the demonstrative “ces” is unclear: is this a generalized prospective


<!-- Page 5 -->


5

warning to avoid the conventional figure of the losengiers, stereotypical enemies of courtly

love? Or is this a specific retrospective casting of the last-mentioned subject in the previous

stanza, l’Amant, as a false lover? There is insufficient precision to be clear, but more than

sufficient ambiguity to be suggestive. Ladies are exhorted, with greater referential clarity, not

to imitate the cruelty of the Dame:

Celle que m’oyez nommer cy,

Qu’on peut appeller, se me semble,

La belle dame sans mercy (798-800)

[“This lady whom you will now hear me name, / and who should be called, it seems to

me, / the Belle Dame Sans Mercy”].

It is striking how much l’Acteur inflects this verdict with markers of subjectivity

underlining his individual perspective – the repeated first-person pronoun, the double

concession of possibility (“qu’on peut”) and seeming (“semble”). Read in isolation, the markers

admit the limitations of his own experience, as when, two stanzas earlier, he grants that his

knowledge of l’Amant’s death was uncertain (“depuis ne sceüs qu’il devint,” [777: “I do not

know what became of him afterward”]) because only hearsay (“[…] on me rapporta / […] /

Qu’il en estoit mort de courroux,” [781, 784: “[…] someone told me / […] / that finally he had

died of his distress”]). But they do not attenuate the authority of his judgment: in the context of

the querelle responses that ensue, his condemnatory labeling of the lady definitionally and

definitively fixes her identity, and her suitor’s death is treated by most respondents as

unequivocal fact. Unlike Machaut’s jugement narrators, Chartier’s does not defer judgment to

a third party, but delivers it himself; the consequence for the extratextual audience, however, is

a not dissimilar solicitation of our assessment of that verdict’s validity and of l’Acteur’s

capacity for sound judgment given the frailties, emotional biases, and melancholic inclinations

that he manifested before assuming his role as aural witness (Armstrong and Kay 131).


<!-- Page 6 -->


6

Subjective judgment is key to the querelle: of the twenty or so responses to BDSM that

accrue by 1440, the majority of the most narratively and discursively developed texts adopt a

courtroom fiction to try and re-try la Dame’s alleged culpability for murder. They offer

“selective judicialized re-readings” (Bouchet 330) of the poem which, whilst cultivating

through their legal apparatus an expectation of dispassionate forensic analysis, in fact

underscore the absence of any objective measure of truth, most virtuosically in Achille Caulier’s

La Cruelle femme en amours (CF). Personified Verité, a barrister, is called upon to account for

having supported la Dame’s cause (as occurred in the anonymous “Dame lealle en amours”

(1426-30)), and alleges a remarkable twist of illegitimate impersonation:

Celle qui se mist en mon nom

Pour ceste cause soustenir

Ne fut aultre que Fiction.

Poëterie lui fist venir

Et ma semblable devenir (CF, 329-33)

[“The one who presented herself in my name / in order to defend the lady’s case / was

none other than Fiction, conjured up by Poetry, to appear in my image”]

In a moment of consummate metafictional maneuvering, Caulier evokes the nature of

subjecthood in the querelle: identity is not a given; it is subject to constant mutation (“se

transmüa,” [334: “transfigured”]), construction and recomposition. It is only ever a subjective

judgment, by the person perceiving themselves or by an “aultre” who perceives them: for

example, there is no “belle dame sans mercy” prior to l’Acteur’s gesture of bringing into being

through naming in BDSM, and that naming remains an allegation, a challengeable judgment

call. Hence the potential for endless propagation of debate.

Subject boundaries in the querelle


<!-- Page 7 -->


7

Caulier manifests a particular predilection for disrupting boundaries in his two querelle

contributions, CF and L’Ospital d’amours (before 1441, OA). CF’s opening dream vision

experienced by l’Acteur strikes something of a keynote: he encounters a metamorphic palace

of uncertain spatial dimensions, temporally conflating past, present and future, and decorated

on all surfaces with shape-shifting images: “voit on de chacun sa figure / Transmüer en estas

divers” (CF 127-8: “and each figure metamorphosed / from one form to another and back

again”). This vision represents the tensions of subjecthood suspended in formation between one

and many possibilities, between sameness and difference, such that l’Acteur cannot isolate a

single figure: “n’y pos mon regard arrester / Sur une chose […]” (118-19: “I could not fix my

eye / on a single thing […]”). Such a relational, mutational principle is applied by Caulier in

OA to the figures of l’Acteur and l’Amant of BDSM, regarding the point of view that each offers

on the love debate. OA opens unlike many other responses: its Acteur is not melancholic, but is

“assés joyeulx” (OA 1: “amply joyful”); he attends a courtly gathering in good cheer,

approaches the lady to whom he is devoted and boldly discloses his ardor, which she rejects;

he persists, but eventually loses hope in the face of reiterated refusals. Grief-stricken, he

surrenders himself to being an amant martir, and then has a dream vision which embarks him

on the journey to the hospital of Love that constitutes the main body of the poem. OA’s Acteur

thus slips into the role of BDSM’s Amant, but rewound to a point in time when l’Amant first

approached the Dame, prior to BDSM’s debate, such that OA’s opening offers the “backstory”

of his amorous grief – the emotional state in which we encounter him in BDSM pleading with

the Dame – told here from l’Amant’s perspective. There is bathetic humor in Caulier’s

mutational maneuver, not least in reducing the history of the affair from seventy-two stanzas of

reported speech to merely four of narrative summary: “Sur quoy elle me respondy / En petiz de

motz, grant reffuz” (47-8: “And she gave me her response: / in a few short words, she rejected

me soundly”). Through pithy antithesis, “petiz” vs. “grant,” he crisply summarises the extended

debate. The tone in which OA’s Acteur-Amant recounts the Dame’s refusal is resigned: no


<!-- Page 8 -->


8

emotional interjections or self-pitying rhetoric: “Finablement tant la requis / Que de m’oÿr plus

se lassa” (49-50: “By the end, I had pled with her for so long / that she tired of listening to me”).

The simplicity of this narrative account, declining to offer judgment, suggesting the logical

consequence of the Dame (reasonably) tiring of his (unreasonable) importuning, casts his amant

martir self-styling (“mieulx amoit mourir que vivre,” [64: “even preferring death to life”]) as

comically disproportionate – it invites us to judge him.

Redirection of audience judgment towards l’Amant and l’Acteur is not unique to

Caulier’s OA. An anonymous querelle contribution that similarly plays reflexively with the

parameters of the debate is the Debat sans conclusion (DSC). Its discursive scenario of debate

between Amant and Dame, relayed by an eavesdropping Acteur, picks up directly that of

BDSM. Instead of an allegorical courtroom drama about them, we re-encounter them in person,

in a re-run that could pick up straight after BDSM, with l’Amant’s opening sally, “Pour vous

seule la mort m’assault” (JdP fol. 149r: “for you alone death strikes me down”). He presses her,

after eighty-four stanzas, for “final response / Avant que plus vivre renonce” (fol. 152v: “a final

answer / before I decide not to live any longer”), but, as she opens her mouth to reply, a stag

appears and the pair move out of earshot to where the hunt is arriving. DSC is an extraordinarily

deft remaniement of BDSM; the dialogue never quotes exactly Chartier’s characters’ discourse,

but reformulates their points with renewed emphasis in two areas: l’Amant’s wilful self-

fashioning as a martyr for love, and la Dame’s resistance to the relationality in which he tries

to trap her. L’Amant’s very first words capture his deterministic attitudes towards identity: “Je

suis celluy / Vers qui Fortune crie a luy” (fol. 149r: “I am the one / towards whom Fortune cries

out”): he attributes his destiny, “sur qui je n’ay quelque puissance” (fol. 150r: “over which I

have not the slightest control”), to the jurisdiction of assorted third-party authorities: la Dame,

Fortune, apostrophized Death. He is made, metaleptically, to recognize the bootlessness of such

discourse: “Et quant j’auray tout debatu / Si ne gaigneray je ung festu” (fol. 151v: “and once I

have debated everything / I will gain nothing”). The DSC author seems to suggest that part of


<!-- Page 9 -->


9

l’Amant’s problem is that he is in the wrong mode: a lyric lover stuck in a narrative world,

endlessly circling through lamentation: “puisque sans fin mercy crier” (fol. 152v: “since I

ceaselessly implore mercy”). His discourse reads as a collation of lyric utterances (“Je suis

[faicte] pour vivre et languir,” [fol. 150v: “I am [made] to live and languish”]), and, in one

passage of dialogue, similarity between the last lines of three successive stanzas suggests a

refrain, in the manner of a jeu-parti (“Si fault que mercy je vous crie,” “Que homme juste crie

mercy,” “Suis je contrant que mercy crie,” [fol. 150v: “And I must implore mercy from you,

That a just man implores mercy, I am obliged to implore mercy”]). Contrariwise, the Dame is

keen to move on, but finds narrative progress obstructed by her obdurate interlocutor: “Car

vostre dueil riens ne m’avance” (fol. 149v: “For your grief does not move me forward at all”).

L’Amant pronounces judgment on her, casting her as his cruel murderer, in line with those

querelle responses that condemn BDSM’s Dame as guilty: “[…] cruaulté, de voz meurs guide,

/ Vous fera de moy homicide” (fol. 151r: “[…] cruelty, which guides your conduct, / will make

you my murderer”). He plots a single path for her identity that determines, and thereby

validates, his self-fashioning as amant martir. He also configures her as his unique object of

desire and thus the sole subject (“vous seule”) to save him; she resists this exclusive

relationality. Her early riposte, “Je ne suis vostre ne vous mien” (fol. 149r: “I am not yours, nor

you mine”) rebuts precisely BDSM’s Amant’s avowal: “Je suis vostre et vostre me tien” (204:

“I declare and consider myself yours”). She posits instead a model of generalized, inclusive

benevolence, “honneste commune amitié / Sans point de specialitié” (fol. 149v: “honourable

shared amity / without any particularity”), which thus implicitly establishes her as universally

sympathetic rather than singularly merciless: “J’ayme chascun et vous aussi” (fol. 152v: “I love

everyone, including you”).

What judgment is imposed by DSC’s Acteur? As in BDSM, an affinity with l’Amant is

evoked, here indirectly rather than through explicit self-alignment: on first sighting him at the

start, l’Acteur adopts twice the same discourse privileging singularity (“Par especial en vis je


<!-- Page 10 -->


10

ung,” “Et par especial [ce]luy,” [ fol. 148v: “I saw one in particular, And particularly this one”]).

His commentary after the debate both echoes and diverges from BDSM, as his eavesdropping

posture receives an ironic twist: the convention for this position, as we saw in Chartier’s poem,

was for obscured vision to be offset by clear audition; at the end of DSC, this gets ironically

reversed when the interlocutors move away to the lake: “Veoye bien qu’ilz devisoient / Mais je

ne scay ce qu’ilz disoient” (fol. 153v: “I could clearly see that they were talking / but I do not

know what they were saying”). The ultimate frustration! He consequently embraces the same

nescience as BDSM’s Acteur: “Si ne sceu que chascun devint” (fol. 153r: “I do not know what

became of each of them”), and offers a conclusion similarly biased towards l’Amant’s interests,

albeit expressed in impersonal, sentential terms rather than as a subjective verdict applied

directly: “On est malement fortuné / Qu’en la fin sera guerdonné” (fol. 153r: “He who suffers

ill fortune / in the end will be rewarded”). He seems implicitly to affirm the validity of

l’Amant’s self-stylization as powerless victim and to justify persistence in his suit. L’Acteur’s

discourse thus demonstrates inconsistency between insistence on particularity (“par especial”)

and recourse to a general rule, which raises a question mark over his reliability and also

highlights other disjunctures: he brands la Dame’s manner of speech “froidement” (“coldly”),

when its content (“J’ayme chascun en sa bonté,” [ fol. 149v: “I love everyone for their virtue”])

bespeaks sympathy.3 This might remind us of la Dame’s own interjection of caution:

Congnoistre homme a sa parole

Seroit plus miracle que sens.

Tous ont esté a une escole (fol. 152r)

[“To be able to know a man by his word / would be more miracle than common sense.

/ They have all come from the same school”]

– should we be questioning l’Acteur’s word as well as l’Amant’s?

DSC’s Acteur becomes an even more intriguing first-person subject when viewed in the

context of the poem’s transmission, which varies both the textual ending of the poem and its


<!-- Page 11 -->


11

co-textuality, thereby underscoring the aptness of its title for its fluctuating boundaries. Extant

as a discrete item in three manuscripts (Paris, Arsenal 3523; Brussels, Bib. Roy., 0969; Turin,

Bibl. Naz. Univ., L.IV.3 (destroyed 1904)) and one incunable, JdP, it was also incorporated as

a discursive episode within the narrative of La Chasse d’Amours (CA), an 8828-line allegorical

tale of amorous hunting, itself preserved in no manuscript copies, but included in a 1509

anthology printed by Antoine Vérard, also the first publisher of JdP. Arsenal 3523 is a late-15th

century compilation of mostly narrative poetry related to the BDSM querelle and, more broadly

in thematic terms, to death. DSC is, ironically appropriately, the final item (fol. 793r: Cayley

200-1), immediately following L’Ambusche Vaillant, otherwise known as Le Debat des deux

seurs, by Vaillant, which stages an acquisitive narrator eavesdropping on two sisters’

conversation: “Pour mieulx leur savoir reproucher / Au lendemain tout le chant d’elles” (fol.

759r, 7-8: “The better to be able to reproach them / the following day for all their talk”). Such

self-serving mischief may be seen similarly to color DSC’s Acteur, who states his intent at the

poem’s outset: “pour avoir du deduit ma part” (JdP, fol. 148v: “to have my share of fun”);

“embusché” (“ambushed”) features figuratively at least twice in DSC’s interlocutors’ discourse,

with evident dramatic irony given their ignorance of his literal eavesdropping presence. A

curious feature of DSC in the Arsenal manuscript is a reworking of the title: “La conclusion du

debat sans relacion” (fol. 793r: “the end of the debate without report”): is this simply accidental

scribal inversion or an interestingly intentional gesture, by the compiler, to the poem’s

ironically unfulfilled eavesdropper who, as we saw above, ultimately fails to overhear?

In JdP, the role of DSC’s narrator is underscored pictorially by a prefatory woodcut

whose two generic figures are labeled “Amours” (“Love”) and “Le relateur” (“The reporter”),

beneath a title-rubric: “La relation faicte au jardin de plaisance du debat de l’amant de la dame

qui est sans conclusion” (148r: “The report made in the pleasure garden of the debate between

the lover and the lady which is without end”). The title’s oblique formulation, like that for the

following item, “Le racomptement fait au jardin de plaisance de deux amans fortunez d’amour”


<!-- Page 12 -->


12

(fol. 153r: “The account made in the pleasure garden of the two lovers’ fortunes in love”),

highlights a tale’s need for a teller, who is pictured as “L’acteur” in the woodcut accompanying

this second poem, Chartier’s Debat de deux fortunés d’amours (1412-14?, DDF). The reader

of both is thus primed to privilege the narrator’s role in their interpretation of the text. Whereas

the discursive scenario of Chartier’s DDF is summarised visually with “L’acteur” alongside

“L’amant,” “Le relateur” of DSC is shown alongside “Amours,” an authority referenced in the

interlocutors’ debate, but not featuring as a personified character in the fiction. This invites us

to refer back to the two items immediately preceding DSC in JdP, Baudet Herenc’s Parlement

d’amours (1425-26) and Caulier’s CF, both querelle contributions deploying full juridical

allegorical scaffolding, as indicated in the latter’s title-rubric, “Comment au jardin de plaisance

est baillé sentence en la court d’amours contre la belle dame sans mercy” (fol. 142v: “How, in

the pleasure garden, sentence is granted in the court of love against the Belle Dame Sans

Mercy”). JdP’s compiler places value on sequentiality and continuousness (Taylor 286), which

manifests itself paratextually, but also textually, in the striking juxtaposition of DSC’s closing

narratorial aphorism, “on est malement fortuné” (“he who suffers ill fortune”), with DDF’s

title-rubric. As mentioned above, DSC’s Amant is at pains to present himself as superlatively

misfortuned:

Triste, mauldit, infortuné,

Et la honte des malheureux

Suis-je, devant tout homme né (fol. 150r)

[“sad, cursed, ill-fated, / and the shame of the wretched / am I, above any living man”].

It is once again a relational matter: the individual claims their singularity whilst at the

same time setting themselves up as an exemplary type; this thereby shifts us into a measure of

generality, and the “on” of DSC’s inconclusive concluding sententia effects a shift into broader

referentiality that can then be narrowed again situationally into the “deux parties” (fol. 156r:

“two parties”) of DDF.


<!-- Page 13 -->


13

The figure of the lover and his representative role are drawn into focus in CA, which

affords l’Amant the most decisive condemnation of any BDSM querelle contribution, and also

situates his conduct in the broader context of the querelle des femmes. DSC’s insertion into CA

(4661-5651) carries the section rubric: “La Dame sans pitié et l’Amant Oultrecuydé; et l’Acteur

qui regard le tout et dit” (207: “The pitiless Lady and the Presumptuous Lover; and the Narrator

who observes it all and writes”). L’Amant is thus framed as a negative exemplum, with his

pejorative epithet included in each speaker-rubric; its pertinence stems from a ten-stanza,

intercalated misogynistic invective that he issues at the end of the debate. It is important to

recognize, however, that these stanzas do not freshly transform l’Amant’s discourse so much

as extend and intensify a vein already evidenced in two earlier vituperative outbursts to la

Dame: “Ha, dur cueur, remply de rigueur” (4877: “Ah, hard heart, filled with cruelty”) and

“Mais vostre langue est affaictee / Com couleuvre à mordre affectee” (5514-15: “but your

tongue is poised / like a viper ready to bite”).4 The implied positive counterpoint to l’Amant

Oultrecuydé is CA’s narrative protagonist l’Amant Parfait (“the Perfect Lover”); l’Acteur of the

inserted DSC is thus fused with the overall narrator of CA and castigates l’Amant Oultrecuydé

as a false lover – one to whom DSC’s sentential conclusion, “on est […] qu’en la fin sera

guerdonné,” (fol. 153r: “he […] in the end will be rewarded”) would thus presumably not apply.

Whilst the most straightforward reading is certainly to see l’Amant Oultrecuydé as “un contre-

modèle de l’Amant Parfait” (CA, p. xl), one might also consider whether, in the manner of a

Fortuna bifrons, he is not so discretely differentiated: “Parfait’ and ‘Oultrecuydé” would, in that

optic, stand as alternative perspectives on the same figure – when does devotion become

obsession, earnestness become overweaning ardor? It is also the case that l’Acteur’s decrial of

l’Amant Oultrecuydé is not as clear-cut as might at first seem, and does not preclude criticism

also of la Dame. Whilst he denounces him for “tromperie” (5586: “deception”) – epitomizing

the figure of the untrustworthy man delineated by la Dame – he defines l’Amant’s

presumptuousness as misplaced belief rather than deceptive guile: he is “oultrecuydé”:


<!-- Page 14 -->


14

D’ainsi avoir avoit cuydé

L’amour de ceste belle dame

Qui onc ne l’ayma par mon ame (5576-8)

[“for having thus believed in / the love of this beautiful lady / who never loved him, by

my soul”].

Switching focus to la Dame, l’Acteur reiterates his assertion unequivocally: “Onc ne luy

monstra amytié, / Mais rudesse et inimité” (5582-3: “she never showed him amity, / but rather

harshness and enmity”), but can we “congnoistre […] a sa parole” (P) this man either? CA’s

interpolated invective also includes a single-stanza response by la Dame to the voluble Amant’s

ten, which underlines her avowal of inclusive benevolence: “Je vous respons que sur mon ame

/ Vous et tout chascun tresfort j’ayme” (5530-1: “I answer you that, upon my soul, / I love very

dearly you and everyone else”). This is surely not “never” showing “any” love, even if one

adheres doggedly to l’Amant’s restricted understanding of “especial” love.

DSC thus discursively creates a counterpoint to CA’s protagonist through its debate; it

also slots readily into the poem’s narrative structure through its existing book-ending

adumbration of a hunt scenario, with l’Acteur’s reference in the opening stanza to overhearing

“trompes et chiens” (“horns and dogs”) and the closing narrative device of the distracting deer.

CA as a whole offers two answers to the question of who or what is being hunted and who is

doing the hunting: there is a double object – the “cerf” (“deer”) who is the stag whose pursuit

structures the narrative, and, through homophony, the “serf” (“servant”) who is l’Amant being

initiated into love’s service by Cupid’s officers. DSC raises at least two further answers: la

Dame and the reader. In the copies in which DSC features as a discrete item, and thus does not

need to elaborate a continuing hunt narrative, a summary conclusion is imposed on the chase:

“Illec fut la beste tenue / Et prinse a force devenue” (fol. 152v: “there was the animal captured

/ and taken by force”). Designating the captured quarry “la beste” evokes a number of potential

referents: the deer itself, of course, but also, metaphorically, the desiring Amant – is he caught


<!-- Page 15 -->


15

in the snares of his own melancholic devotion? La Dame deploys hunting metaphors in the

course of their debate, advising him, “vos fillez autre part tendez” (fol. 150r: “cast your nets

elsewhere”) and declaring “oncques es latz d’amours n’entray” (fol. 152v: “I shall never enter

the snares of love”); she thus seems to preclude herself from capture, but the grammatical

femininity of “la beste” offers the possibility of her having nonetheless been taken by force,

against her will. Or is love itself – labeled in DSC’s woodcut illustration in JdP – ensnared,

which we as audience are tracking through the text and its co-texts? JdP’s rudimentary narrative

framework outlines a wander through a garden wherein several tales entertain a coursing

situation, such as “une chasse appellee la pipee au dieu d’amours” (fol. 187v: “a course called

the hunt of the god of Love”). Are we as readers the hunters, watching for hermeneutic traps?

We recall, for instance, the use of a hunting metaphor to depict the activity of judges in BDSM:

“leurs juges […] / Qui les tiennent en leurs liens” (79-80: “their judges, […] who held them in

thrall”). What might ensnare our understanding?

Identity formation through “ung autre”

DSC’s Dame supports her case for refusing Amant’s advances through allusive

reference to unhappy precedents: “J’ay bien des autres souvenir / Qui ont perdu honneur et

gloires” (fol. 152r: “I have a clear memory of others / who have lost honour and glory”). But

she names none, which is highly unusual for querelle debates, and for late-medieval dits more

generally, often awash with enumerated exempla from an array of sources: biblical, Classical

and contemporary; mythological, legendary and historical. Such citational practice plays an

important role in first-person identity formation: from the speaker’s perspective, it is part of

their self-fashioning, defining themselves in relation to cases that stand as models, such as Echo,

Thisbe, or Dido as tragic victims of love; from the implied authorial perspective, it offers the

possibility for character critique, with the reader invited to assess how appropriately or

rhetorically successfully the speaker shapes their self-presentation, as in Machaut’s JRN


<!-- Page 16 -->


16

(Blumenfeld-Kosinski 142). Chartier’s Dame and Amant themselves become mythemes,

commonplaces of contemporary mythography, like the protagonists of the 13th century

Chastelaine de Vergy.

Le Purgatoire d’amours (PA), a late querelle contribution attributed to Pierre Michault

and dated in manuscript copies to 1463, dramatizes the construction of a lover’s identity. Before

Cupid’s court, its Amant requests the return of his heart, casting himself as an amant martir and

supporting his case with over twenty exemplary lovers tormented by “les dons d’amours […] /

Jusques a la mort” (JdP, fol. 185v: “the gifts of love […] / until their death”), from Old

Testament Sarah to the Amants of both BDSM and OA. Exceptionally, in the context of querelle

juridical dramas, he gets to plead his case himself rather than being represented posthumously

by others. The verdict does not, however, fall in his favor: Cupid concludes that he is an

impudent, impatient servant, and thus not a “vray amant” (fol. 185r: “true lover”), akin to CA’s

Amant Oultrecuydé, though PA’s Acteur aligns him more to l’Amant Parfait: “si suis certain

que cest amant est pur” (fol. 187r: “I am certain that this lover is pure”). PA’s Amant is

disciplined by three days of punishment in purgatory. Cupid thereby metes out a corrective

lesson that, retrospectively, could have saved BDSM’s Amant from his obstinate pursuit of the

Belle Dame and thereby changed the whole course of the querelle.

L’Amant’s self-defense is offered for our critical consideration: the dreaming Acteur

who witnesses the courtroom scene notes prefatorily that “il par sa parole / Monstra assez qu’il

venoit de l’escolle” (fol. 184r: “he by his speech / demonstrated amply that he came from [that]

school”); we recall DSC’s Dame’s caution that this itself may be reason for skeptical scrutiny.

Amant introduces his argumentative method: “Vray compteray ou les histoires mentent / Car

ja du mien n’y mettray quelque chose” (fol. 185r-185v: “I shall tell the truth where the stories

lie / since I shall not add in anything of my own”). From his point of view, the chiastically

emphasized antithesis underscores the truth value of exempla which he posits as objective and

univocal; for the reader, such a categorical distinction and proclaimed elimination of


<!-- Page 17 -->


17

subjectivity sound a warning bell signaling the speaker’s discursive and narratorial ignorance.

Argument and storytelling have no impersonal truth, as was demonstrated earlier on in PA when

l’Amant first presented his case: it was initially received by President Loyaulté who, on seeking

colleagues’ counsel, “a fin de mieulx la verité scavoir” (fol.183v: “in order better to know the

truth”), received multiple, irreconcilable views: “la diversité / D’oppinions et divers jugemens”

(fol. 183v: “the diversity / of opinions and conflicting judgments”); at a loss how to resolve

them, he deferred upwards to Cupid.

The necessary selectivity in l’Amant’s catalogue of exempla already manifests “du mien

[…] quelque chose” (fol. 185v: “something of my own”), and not always competently – for

instance, confusedly presenting Echo and Narcissus as equal victims. He also imposes

subjective interpretation in his enlistment of BDSM:

L’amant priant la dame sans mercy

Finablement mourut en desespoir.

Ung autre fut prouchain de mort aussi

Ayant le cueur de mesme mercy

Quant il trouva en l’ospital espoir. (PA, fol. 186r)

[“The lover who implored the merciless lady / ultimately died in despair. / Another was

also close to death, / with a heart similarly [seeking] mercy / when he found hope in the

hospital”]

Predictably for a “languissant douloureux” (fol. 184r: “languishing wretch”), he presents

the death of Chartier’s Amant as established fact, and aligns him with Caulier’s to construct a

succession of amant martir antecedents in contemporary culture. The designation “ung autre”

is repeated to introduce each new analog, rendering the referents allusive and soliciting

audience interpretation to identify them, such as “ung aultre amoureux” (“another lover”):

Par [amour morte] a vostre occasion

Il monstra bien qu’il estoit douloureux


<!-- Page 18 -->


18

Quant il vous dist tant de motz rigoreux (fol. 186r )

[“dying for love by your doing, / he truly showed that he was wretched / when he spoke

to you so many harsh words”].

Is this intended to designate an individual case? Is an intertextually alert audience

invited to propose likely candidates, such as the speaker of Chartier’s Complainte (“Las! Or

n’ay plus ce que j’avoye, Amors,” [22: “Alas! Now I no longer have what I had, Love”])? On

the one hand, Amant’s slip into allusiveness seems contrary to his objective of unequivocal

enumeration, and thus a point of discursive weakness; on the other, the plurality of possible

referents across the corpus of medieval dits serves to accrete an ever-expanding body of

examples to buttress his argument. Viewed metatextually, his “ung autre” method draws

attention to the intertextual relationality of typified dit-lover identity: whilst it marks a shift

from one distinct case to another, it nevertheless points to the continuity linking them together

as a chain of related cases, suggesting an approach to the boundaries of subjecthood privileging

permeability and mutation, not discrete distinction.

The richest reading of PA is afforded, as it was for DSC, by examination in its material

context, which in early print transmission likewise includes JdP: “Comment au jardin de

plaisance l’amoureux est au purgatoire d’amours et privé de joye” (fol. 182v: “How, in the

pleasure garden, the lover is in the purgatory of love and deprived of happiness”). JdP’s

anthologisation of courtly love poetry offers particular, cross-textual candidates for PA’s

“autres,” most especially with reference to the series of amant martir items at the volume’s

close, including George Chastelain’s Oultré d’amours (before 1450), Pierre de Hauteville’s La

Confession et testament de l’amant trespassé de dueil (1441-47), concluded by an anonymous

Epitaphe dedicated, with similar allusiveness, to “l’oultré d’amour pour amour morte” (fol.

258v: “the one overcome by love who died for love”). The poems’ title-rubrics foster

interconnection: de Hauteville’s Confession’s picks up Chastelain’s Oultré’s protagonist,

“Comment le chevalier oultré d’amours trespasse de dueil de sa dame” (fol. 247r: “How the


<!-- Page 19 -->


19

knight overcome by love dies of grief for his lady”), who is then carried through into the

Epitaphe’s text, adumbrating progression from life to death, but in sketchy, gestural terms,

passing through, in each fiction, a specific discursive and narrative situation.

Their inclusion in JdP opens up cross-textual resonances for both DSC and PA. In both,

a speaker evokes the arc of an amant martir’s trajectory that one could see to be traced across

the volume: DSC’s Dame advises l’Amant:

Car l’amour de quoy vous usez

Est de fol commencement

Et de si triste finement (fol. 152r)

[“the love that you practise / has a foolish beginning / and a very sad ending”];

and Cupid counsels PA’s Amant: “Et pour brief, oncques amant, tant fust fin, / Ne me

servit sans doloreuse fin” (fol. 185r: “in sum, no lover, however shrewd, / ever served me

without a wretched end”). The “oultree [or ‘oultrecudyee’?] folie” (fol. 152r: “overwhelming

[or ‘overweaning’?] foolishness”) of DSC’s Amant anticipates “l’oultré d’amours” (fol. 258v:

“the one overcome by love”) of the anthology’s close, whose demise fulfils PA’s promise of

“doloreuse fin”. Paratextually, the title-rubrics promote narrative movement both spatially,

around the putative garden, and temporally, through the lover’s amorous experience and

decline; they outline, therefore, ‘le mouvement biographique de la compilation’ (Frieden, “Le

Jardin de plaisance”), but the nature of that biographical movement needs careful

understanding – it is not purely linear, given, for instance, how DSC’s lexically prominent

“infortuné” resonates with the figure designated as the author of JdP’s opening versification

treatise: “l’infortuné” (fol. A2v: “the ill-fated”); nor is it exclusive to a single figure, but, like

DSC’s Dame’s affections, is inclusive of each “autre” together in a collective coherence:

“chascun et vous aussi” (“everyone, including you”).

Whilst there is no individuality of identity, there is nonetheless specificity in the

discursive situation of each text, as indexed by the other organizing paratextual feature of JdP,


<!-- Page 20 -->


20

its woodcuts. Each offers “une contextualisation énonciative immédiate” (Buron 222) of the

poem it prefaces, but direct ontological representation does not individualise. The generic

nature of each human embodiment of “l’Acteur,” “le chevalier,” “le prisoner,” or “l’Amant,”

labeled to identify the particular type concerned (with those types nonetheless being porous and

not mutually exclusive), instantiates the principle of each “autre amoureux” of courtly love

narrative. Like DSC’s Amant’s self-presentation as superlatively cursed, “infortuné / […] /

Suis-je devant tout homme né,” the first-person lover defines himself as set apart from everyone

else, and at the same time cannot define himself except with reference to everyone else, hence

my privileging of relationality as the key concept for understanding subjectivities in formation

in late-medieval dits.

Boundaries of form in JdP

JdP compiles narrative and lyric poetry. As I noted above in respect of the jeu-parti

moment in DSC’s debate, and the interpenetration between Chartier’s Complainte and BDSM,

the boundary between these forms is not fixed. A particular case in point is an item in-between

DSC and PA, entitled “La complainte du prisonnier d’amours faicte au jardin de plaisance” (fol.

161r: “The lament of the prisoner of love made in the pleasure garden”), which comprises

fourteen rondeaux by Chartier presented each as a stanza of the composite complaint. Each

voices a disconsolate love lament, with the title-rubric perhaps deriving from the opening of the

third rondeau/stanza: “Au povre prisonnier, ma dame” (fol. 161r: “to this poor prisoner, my

lady”). Recalling l’Amant’s predicament in DSC, they express a typically lyric stuck-ness, an

inability to move forward narratively, and instead cycle discursively around the same

oxymoronic state: “Je n’ay povoir de vivre en joye / Et si ne puis mourir de dueil” (fol. 161v:

“I cannot live in happiness / and I cannot die of grief”). A peculiarity of JdP is its double table

of contents at the end of the anthology: the first, of (mostly) narrative items that lists the title-

rubrics in chronological order through the volume; the second, which indexes individual lyrics


<!-- Page 21 -->


21

alphabetically by first line, form by form (ballades, rondeaux, chansons, etc.). “La complainte”

features in the former, which prompts us to consider the extent to which there is any meaningful

distinction between the first-person lover-speaker of lyric and narrative items when the self-

fashioning of that persona is as an amant martir. Dying, of course, marks progression, but the

transition itself is never experienced narratively: it is only ever discursively anticipated (and

then, most often, like the favor desired of the beloved, as a longed-for but feared, unknowable

outcome – “Ou mon desir s’assouvira / Ou ma tristesse m’occira,” fol. 161r: “Either my desire

will overwhelm me / or my sorrow will kill me”) or recalled in lamentation by a third party, as

in the Epitaphe for “l’oultré d’amours pour amour morte.”

One distinguishing textual feature of narrative items is the presence of an Acteur, whose

work of framing the tale may be narrative and/or discursive, and may, in the author’s interests

of generating debate about the debate staged within a poem, be deployed to prompt disjuncture

rather than coherence, such as dispensing judgment that sits at odds with events or character

presentation, like PA’s conviction that its punished Amant is a true lover. L’Acteur does not,

therefore, figure the extratextual audience’s point of view: they position themselves at one

remove from his “je”: overhearing him eavesdropping, witnessing him spying. Articulation of

the overall story, that which includes all the first-persons of a given tale and, in an anthology,

interrelation with its cross-textual “autres,” requires the extratextual audience as “relateur”:

without them, the debate is “sans relacion”; it is always, and most productively, “sans

conclusion.”
